dossiers.role-etat.hook: France collects more than 42% of its wealth in taxes and social contributions, and its public administrations spend 57% of GDP. To do what? When does the market manage on its own, and when is the state needed? Who really pays a tax, why is there so little tax fraud in Denmark, and which spending pays for itself? The big ideas of public economics, with concrete examples.
dossiers.role-etat.tldr.0: In 2024, taxes and social contributions amount to 42.8% of GDP in France according to INSEE; using the European method, France ranks 2nd in the EU, just behind Denmark [1][2]. Public spending reaches 57% of GDP, 41% of which goes to social protection (excluding health) [4].
dossiers.role-etat.tldr.1: The state steps in first when the market fails: public goods that no one would pay for alone, pollution whose cost no one pays, risks that private insurers cover poorly because of hidden information [5][6].
dossiers.role-etat.tldr.2: The person who hands over a tax is not always the one who bears it (“tax incidence”), and a tax you don't see on the price tag changes behavior less: displaying the tax cuts purchases by about 8% [7].
dossiers.role-etat.tldr.3: There is very little fraud when a third party reports income (0.3% in Denmark), and much more when people report it themselves (37%) [8]. And some public spending, especially on children from low-income families, pays for itself [9].
dossiers.role-etat.tldr.4: The state also has a cost: every tax changes behavior, the state can get things wrong, and a tax seen as unfair can be rejected, like the carbon tax in 2018 [3].
dossiers.role-etat.sections.0.title: How much does the state collect?
dossiers.role-etat.sections.0.paragraphs: ==Compulsory levies== are all the taxes and social contributions that households and businesses must pay: income tax, VAT, CSG, pension and health contributions, corporate tax, property tax… In France, they amount to ==42.8% of GDP in 2024== according to INSEE, after a record 45.4% in 2022, the highest level measured since 1959 [1].
Using Eurostat's European method, which is slightly broader, the French rate reaches 45.3% in 2024: ==the 2nd highest in the European Union, behind Denmark (45.8%) and ahead of Belgium (45.1%)== [2].

These figures don't tell you whether it is “too much”: they measure how much wealth flows through the state. A large part goes straight back to households as pensions, healthcare reimbursements or benefits. A country with public pensions, like France, mechanically has higher levies than a country where everyone pays into a private pension fund, even if households pay comparable amounts overall.

The real question of public economics, the branch of economics that studies government action and that Raj Chetty teaches at Harvard, is rather: ==in which cases does the state do better than the market, and how should its taxes and spending be designed?==
dossiers.role-etat.sections.1.title: Where does the money go?
dossiers.role-etat.sections.1.paragraphs: In 2024, all public administrations combined (central government, local authorities, Social Security) spend ==about €1,672 billion, or 57% of GDP== [4]. This figure is higher than the levies: the gap is filled by other revenue (sales, income from assets) and above all by the deficit, that is, by debt.

By far the largest item is ==social protection: 41% of spending, or €693 billion== (pensions, unemployment, family, housing, poverty, excluding health) [4]. Pensions are at its core, and they drove most of the increase in spending in 2024 [4].

Next come ==health (16%, €261 billion)== and ==education (9%, €149 billion)== [4]. The rest is shared among general services (including interest on the debt), economic affairs (transport, business support), defense, public order, the environment, housing, culture and sport [4].

Remember the orders of magnitude: ==out of every €100 of public spending, about 41 go to social protection, 16 to health and 9 to schools== [4]. Debates about “savings” therefore necessarily focus on these big items, if you want significant amounts.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.1.example.te: Based on INSEE's breakdown for 2024 [4], €1,000 of public spending splits roughly as follows: €410 for social protection (mostly pensions), €160 for health, €90 for education, and €340 for everything else (general services and interest on the debt, transport, defense, police and justice, the environment, culture…).
dossiers.role-etat.sections.2.title: The main missions of the state
dossiers.role-etat.sections.2.paragraphs: Economists often group government action into three main missions. ==Allocate==: produce or fund what the market produces poorly (roads, research, fighting pollution). ==Redistribute==: reduce income gaps through taxes and benefits. ==Stabilize==: cushion crises by supporting activity when it falls (see our course on the IS-LM model).

This course focuses mainly on the first: ==“market failures”==. These are situations where, even if everyone acts in their own best interest, the result is bad for all. There are three main families: public goods, externalities (such as pollution) and hidden information.

The idea matters because it answers a question that is often badly framed. The point is not whether you are “for” or “against” the state in general, but whether, ==case by case, the market works well and whether the state would do better==. In many areas (bread, clothing, phones), the market works very well on its own.
We will also see that the state has its own failures: lack of information, lobbies, slowness. Comparing always means comparing two imperfect systems.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.3.title: Public goods: what no one would pay for alone
dossiers.role-etat.sections.3.paragraphs: Some goods have two features. You can't stop anyone from benefiting from them (==non-excludability==), and my benefiting from them doesn't deprive others (==non-rivalry==). Examples: street lighting, national defense, a lighthouse for ships, basic research, a flood barrier.

The problem: everyone has an interest in waiting for others to pay, since they will benefit anyway. This is the ==free rider==. As a result, left to the market, this good would be produced in too small a quantity, or not at all, even though everyone wants it.

Hence taxation: the state requires everyone to contribute, and funds what no one would have funded alone. The state doesn't necessarily produce it: a private company can build the flood barrier, but taxes pay for it.

Between purely private goods (your sandwich: rival and excludable) and purely public goods, there are intermediate cases. ==Common goods== are rival, but no one can be excluded: fish in the sea, water in an aquifer. Everyone fishes too much, and the resource runs out. ==Club goods== are non-rival but excludable: a streaming service, a little-used toll motorway. Each category calls for a different solution: fishing quotas, subscriptions, taxes.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.3.plain.step: Your street is dark. A streetlight is expensive, but it benefits all the neighbors.
Each neighbor thinks: “If the others pay, I'll benefit for free.”
No one pays: the street stays dark, even though everyone wanted light.
The town council installs the streetlight and funds it through local taxes: everyone pays a little, and everyone benefits.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.4.title: Pollution: a cost no one pays
dossiers.role-etat.sections.4.paragraphs: When a factory pollutes a river, it imposes a cost on fishers and local residents without paying for it: this is a ==negative externality==. Since this cost doesn't show up in its price, it produces too much. Conversely, a ==positive externality== benefits others without being paid for: a vaccine also protects people who aren't vaccinated, a beehive pollinates neighboring orchards. Left to the market, these activities are too rare.

The classic solution, proposed by British economist Arthur Pigou in “The Economics of Welfare”, is to ==tax pollution at the level of the damage caused==: the polluter then factors this cost into its choices [6]. This is called a “Pigouvian tax”. It is the idea behind the carbon tax (see also our course on the morality of markets). Symmetrically, positive externalities, such as vaccination, can be subsidized.

In 1960, economist Ronald Coase, who went on to win the 1991 Nobel Prize, offered another view in “The Problem of Social Cost” [6]. In his view, the harm is reciprocal: the factory harms the fishers, but banning the factory harms the factory. If property rights are clear and negotiating costs nothing, the parties can reach an agreement among themselves, without a tax, and arrive at an efficient solution [6].

Coase himself acknowledged that these conditions are rarely met: ==when millions of people suffer from pollution, it is impossible to get them all to negotiate==, and “transaction costs” make a private arrangement unrealistic [6]. For the climate, which affects the whole planet, we therefore come back to public tools: taxes, quotas, standards.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.4.plain.titl: Pigou or Coase, on a river
dossiers.role-etat.sections.4.plain.step: A factory dumps waste into a river; a fisher downstream loses €100,000 a year.
Pigou's solution: the state taxes the factory €100,000 a year. If installing a filter is cheaper, it installs one [6].
Coase's solution: if the fisher has a clear right to clean water, the factory can offer him money, or install the filter if that is cheaper. They negotiate on their own [6].
With two parties, Coase works. With millions of residents, negotiating is impossible: we come back to taxes or standards [6].
dossiers.role-etat.sections.5.title: The French carbon tax: effective on paper, rejected in the streets
dossiers.role-etat.sections.5.paragraphs: In France, the carbon tax on energy, called the “climate-energy contribution”, was created in 2014 and raised every year. It reached ==€44.6 per tonne of CO₂ in 2018== [3].
Its planned increase in 2019 was canceled in the face of the yellow vest movement, and it has stayed frozen at that level ever since, whereas the trajectory voted into law aimed for €100 in 2030 [3].

Why was it rejected? Economists draw three lessons. ==It weighs more heavily on low-income and rural households==, who spend a larger share of their income on fuel and heating, and who often have no alternative to the car. ==Its revenue was not visibly returned== to households. And ==it came on top of rising oil prices==, at a time when filling up the tank already cost more.

Other countries chose to redistribute the revenue: in Switzerland, part of the CO₂ tax on heating is paid back to the population. The idea is the same as for the Stockholm congestion charge: ==a price is more readily accepted when people can see what the money is used for==. A tool that is effective in an economist's eyes can be rejected if it seems unfair.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.6.title: Who really pays the tax?
dossiers.role-etat.sections.6.paragraphs: The person who hands the tax over to the state is not always the one who bears its burden: this is the question of ==tax incidence==.

Example: “employer” social contributions are paid by the employer. But if they go up, the company can raise wages less: part of the burden is then borne by employees. Likewise, a tax on a product is often passed on in the price, and so paid by the customer, even though the seller is the one who hands it over.

General rule: ==whoever has the fewest alternatives bears the tax==. If customers can't do without the product (their demand is said to be “inelastic”), they are the ones who pay; if they can easily switch, the seller pays. Tariffs are a good example (see our course on tariffs).

An important consequence: ==you can't decide by law who really pays a tax==. Lawmakers decide who hands it over; markets decide who bears it. That is why a serious debate about taxes always looks at the real effects, not just the name of whoever writes the check.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.6.plain.step: The state raises the tax on each pack; the manufacturer hands it over.
Addicted smokers buy almost as much, even at a higher price.
So the manufacturer raises its price by almost the full amount of the tax.
In the end, it is mostly smokers who pay it, not the manufacturer.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.7.title: The tax you don't see
dossiers.role-etat.sections.7.paragraphs: In the United States, prices displayed in stores exclude tax: sales tax is only added at the checkout. In 2009, Raj Chetty and his colleagues Adam Looney and Kory Kroft asked whether customers really take it into account [7].

They ran an experiment in a supermarket. For three weeks, on about 750 taxable products (cosmetics, hair accessories, deodorants), they added a label showing ==the tax-inclusive price== [7]. Nothing else changed: the price paid at the checkout was exactly the same.

Result: ==sales of these products fell by about 8%==, almost as much as if the price had actually risen by 7.375%, the amount of the tax [7]. Without the label, almost all the customers surveyed forgot the tax when calculating the price of their basket [7].

Economists call this ==“salience”==: a highly visible tax changes behavior more than a hidden one. The consequence for tax incidence and for policy: a hidden tax makes people react less (so it “costs” less in lost activity), but it is also less transparent. And a tax meant to change behavior, such as a tax on tobacco or carbon, works better when it is clearly visible.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.7.plain.step: On the shelf, a deodorant is priced at $4.00. At the checkout, you pay $4.30 with the 7.375% tax.
Most customers only think about the $4.00: the tax is “invisible” [7].
The researchers add a label reading “$4.30 tax included”. The actual price hasn't changed.
Sales fall by about 8%, as if the price had really gone up [7]: what you see matters as much as what you pay.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.8.title: Why people pay their taxes
dossiers.role-etat.sections.8.paragraphs: If tax audits are rare, why do most people pay what they owe? In 2011, a team of economists including Henrik Kleven and Emmanuel Saez published a remarkable study conducted with the Danish tax administration [8].
More than 40,000 Danish taxpayers were selected at random: half underwent a thorough audit, the other half were deliberately not audited [8]. This made it possible to measure fraud precisely.

The result is very clear. On income reported by a third party (wages reported by the employer, interest reported by the bank), ==fraud is almost zero: 0.3%==. On self-reported income (self-employment, some capital income), ==it reaches 37%== [8]. Since 95% of income is reported by a third party in Denmark, overall fraud remains low [8].

The lesson: people are not necessarily more honest in Denmark than elsewhere; ==they pay mainly because they can't easily cheat==. The study's title sums it up: “Unwilling or Unable to Cheat?” France followed the same logic with pay-as-you-earn withholding since 2019 and pre-filled tax returns: when the information comes from a third party, taxes are collected more effectively.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.9.title: Insuring what the market insures poorly
dossiers.role-etat.sections.9.paragraphs: Unemployment, illness, old age: why does the state get involved? Because private insurance works poorly in these areas, due to ==hidden information==.

In 1970, economist George Akerlof published a now-famous article, “The Market for Lemons”, about used cars [5]. The seller knows whether their car is a good vehicle or a “lemon” (a car full of defects); the buyer has no way of knowing. So the buyer offers an average price. Owners of good cars, underpaid, take their cars off the market; only the bad ones remain, and the market can collapse [5]. Akerlof received the Nobel Prize in 2001, together with Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz, for their work on asymmetric information [5].

Insurance faces the same problem. If unemployment insurance were optional, those most afraid of losing their job would sign up first; the insurer would have to raise its prices, the “good risks” would leave, and the system would collapse. This is ==adverse selection==.

By making insurance compulsory for everyone, the state breaks this cycle: everyone contributes, good and bad risks alike. This is the logic of French Social Security. Insurance also creates another problem, ==moral hazard==: once insured, people may be less careful. Hence deductibles, waiting periods and job-search checks, which leave part of the risk with the insured person.
dossiers.role-etat.sections.9.plain.step: A private insurer offers unemployment insurance at €50 a month, calculated on the average risk.
Employees in very secure jobs find it too expensive and don't take it; those who fear being laid off all take it.
The insurer pays out a lot in benefits: it raises the price to €80. More “safe” employees leave.
The cycle continues until only the highest-risk people are left: the insurance disappears. Made compulsory, it holds up, because everyone contributes: this is adverse selection [5].
dossiers.role-etat.sections.10.title: Spending that pays for itself
dossiers.role-etat.sections.10.paragraph: How can you tell whether public spending is worth what it costs? In 2020, Nathaniel Hendren and Ben Sprung-Keyser, from Raj Chetty's lab at Harvard, compared ==133 US public policies== using a single measure, the ==“marginal value of public funds”==: what beneficiaries would be willing to pay for the policy, divided by its net cost to the government [9].

The net cost takes feedback effects into account: if a benefit helps someone find a better job, they will pay more taxes later and receive fewer benefits. Some policies thus have a negative net cost: ==they bring the government more than they cost it==.

The main finding: ==investments in the health and education of children from low-income families have historically had the highest returns==, often more than $5 of value per dollar spent, and many have paid for themselves through taxes paid later and benefits avoided [9]. Spending on adults generally yields less, except when it also benefits their children, like the Moving to Opportunity relocation assistance (see our course on social mobility) [9].

This work changes the debate: instead of pitting “spending” against “saving”, it invites us to ==rank spending by what it returns== to society. Not all policies for children are cost-effective, the authors warn, but the trend is clear [9].
dossiers.role-etat.sections.11.title: The limits: the state also has a cost
dossiers.role-etat.sections.11.paragraph: ==Every tax changes behavior.== A tax on labor can discourage working more, a tax on savings can discourage saving: economists call the wealth lost this way ==“deadweight loss”==. The more the tax base reacts (people who can easily change their behavior or country), the greater the loss. That is why economists often prefer broad-based taxes with moderate rates.

==The state can get things wrong.== It sometimes lacks information, gives in to lobbies or reacts slowly: we speak of “government failures”, just as we speak of market failures. A tax loophole can survive for decades because those who benefit from it mobilize, while its cost is spread across everyone.
==Acceptance matters.== The French carbon tax shows that a good tool on paper is not enough: it has to be seen as fair, and people need to see what the money is used for [3].

==Debt has a price.== When spending exceeds revenue, the state borrows. Interest on the debt is part of public spending [4]: the higher it climbs, the less is left for everything else. Good public spending, like the kind that pays for itself [9], can justify borrowing; routine operating expenses, much less so.
dossiers.role-etat.forMe: Your payslip, your fuel fill-up, your till receipt: they all include levies. Knowing what they are used for (social protection, health, schools, public goods, fighting pollution), who really bears them and why some are better accepted than others helps you judge tax debates without slogans.

dossiers.role-etat.quiz.1.q: What is a public good in the economic sense?
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.1.options.0: A good sold by the state
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.1.options.1: A good from which no one can be excluded and that everyone can use without depriving others
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.1.options.3: A good produced by a state-owned company
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.1.explain: Non-excludability and non-rivalry: a lighthouse, street lighting, defense.
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.2.options.1: A common good: rival, but no one can be excluded
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.2.explain: Everyone fishes too much and the resource runs out: hence fishing quotas.
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.3.options.1: A cost imposed on others without being paid for, like pollution
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.3.explain: The polluter doesn't pay for the damage it causes to others: so it produces too much.
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.4.q: According to Coase, when can private negotiation resolve pollution without a tax?
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.4.options.1: When property rights are clear and negotiating costs almost nothing
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.4.explain: With millions of victims, transaction costs make negotiation impossible: we come back to taxes or standards.
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.5.explain: This is tax incidence: if customers can't do without the product, they pay most of it.
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.6.q: In Chetty's supermarket experiment, what did displaying the tax-inclusive price cause?
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.6.options.1: A drop in sales of about 8%
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.6.options.3: A drop in the price paid
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.6.explain: The price paid hadn't changed: it was the visibility of the tax that made customers react.
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.7.q: Why is tax fraud low in Denmark?
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.7.options.1: 95% of income is reported by a third party (employer, bank)
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.7.explain: Fraud of 0.3% on third-party-reported income, compared with 37% on self-reported income.
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.8.q: Why is optional unemployment insurance likely to collapse?
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.8.options.1: Adverse selection: only the highest-risk people get insured
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.8.explain: Good risks leave, prices rise, the system empties out: making it compulsory breaks this cycle.
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.9.q: According to Hendren and Sprung-Keyser's study, which public spending has the highest returns?
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.9.options.1: Health and education for children from low-income families
dossiers.role-etat.quiz.9.explain: Many have paid for themselves through taxes paid later and benefits avoided.

dossiers.droits-de-douane.tldr.3: The debate is two centuries old: in 1817, David Ricardo showed that two countries gain from trade even if one is better at everything [19]; in 1930, the US Smoot-Hawley Act raised tariffs on more than 20,000 products and triggered retaliation [15].
dossiers.droits-de-douane.tldr.4: After 1947, the GATT and then the WTO (1995) brought global tariffs down [16]. But since December 11, 2019, the WTO Appellate Body, which settles disputes, has been paralyzed by a US blockade [18].
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.5.tit: 1817: why trade, even when you're better at everything
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.5.par: To understand tariffs, you first need to understand why almost all economists defend trade. The key idea comes from English economist ==David Ricardo==, in ==1817==: the theory of ==comparative advantage== [19].

His example has become famous. Portugal produces wine and cloth more efficiently than England: it needs fewer hours of labor for both [19]. Does that mean it should produce everything itself? No, says Ricardo: Portugal is ==much== better at wine, and only ==slightly== better at cloth. If it specializes in wine, England in cloth, and they trade, ==both countries consume more wine and more cloth== than if each produced everything on its own [19].

It is counterintuitive, and that is why it matters: ==a country doesn't need to be the best at something to gain from trade==; it only needs to specialize where its disadvantage is smallest. A tariff, by preventing this specialization, in principle makes both countries poorer.

But the theory has its blind spots: it says the country gains ==overall==, not that everyone gains. Workers in the sector that disappears (here, Portuguese cloth) lose their jobs. All of trade policy revolves around this tension: a diffuse gain for everyone, losses concentrated on a few.
dossiers.droits-de-douane.sections.5.pla: Ricardo's example, in hours of labor
